claims.explanation: Fluspirilene is a diphenylbutylpiperidine antipsychotic that, unlike typical dopamine antagonists, also blocks voltage-gated calcium channels and inhibits CDK2, and it induces autophagy via calpain1/ATG5. Selective killing likely reflects dependence on calcium signaling and/or CDK2/autophagy pathways, with TP53-mutant and KRAS/BRAF-driven lines being more sensitive, while intact PTEN/PI3K-AKT signaling and certain lineage contexts (e.g., some gastric, melanoma, and thyroid lines) confer protection.

features.basis: TP53 mutations are highly enriched among selectively killed lines (18/20) versus least affected lines, consistent with loss of p53-mediated survival and autophagy regulation
KRAS-mutant pancreatic and colorectal lines are among the most killed, suggesting oncogenic KRAS dependence on calcium/CDK2 signaling
BRAF-mutant melanoma lines (K029AX, IGR37) are selectively killed, possibly via MAPK-driven calcium channel dependence
PTEN mutations appear in several least-affected lines (ZR751, UACC62, HEC265), suggesting intact PTEN/AKT signaling may not be required for survival under fluspirilene
Fluspirilene is annotated to target CACNG1 and blocks voltage-gated calcium channels; high expression of calcium channel subunits may increase sensitivity
Fluspirilene is a potent dopamine D2 receptor antagonist; DRD2 expression may contribute to sensitivity in neuroendocrine or other DRD2-expressing tumors
Fluspirilene was identified as a CDK2 inhibitor with anti-proliferative activity; high CDK2 expression may predict sensitivity
Fluspirilene induces autophagy by preventing calpain1-mediated ATG5 cleavage; low full-length ATG5 may limit this effect, so higher ATG5 could enhance sensitivity
Calpain1 cleaves ATG5 and limits autophagy; high calpain1 activity may protect cells from fluspirilene-induced autophagy
EGFR-mutant lung lines (HCC4006, NCIH1650) are among the most killed, suggesting EGFR-driven tumors may depend on calcium signaling
SF3B1 mutations appear in two selectively killed lines (HCC95, UO31), though the mechanism is unclear
NF1 mutations appear in multiple killed lines (BICR6, FTC133, KALS1), possibly via RAS pathway activation
